title: The KVM ioctl lifecycle
hook: What are the `/dev/kvm` ioctls a VMM calls to create and run a vCPU?

scenes.caption: KVM exposes three file-descriptor levels: system, VM and vCPU.
scenes.narration: KVM is driven through file descriptors. Opening dev kvm gives a system fd, and creating a VM returns a VM fd. Creating a vCPU returns a third fd, one per vCPU.

scenes.caption: Setup: create a VM, register guest RAM, create a vCPU.
scenes.narration: A VMM opens dev kvm, creates a VM, registers memory, and creates a vCPU. The memory region maps a slice of the VMM's own address space as guest physical memory.

scenes.caption: A memory slot binds guest physical addresses to the VMM's userspace buffer.
scenes.narration: The region struct names a slot, the guest physical address, the size, and the userspace address of the backing memory. So guest RAM is just anonymous memory in the VMM process.

scenes.caption: Map struct kvm_run from the vCPU fd, then loop on KVM_RUN.
scenes.narration: Each vCPU has a shared kvm_run page, mapped from the vCPU fd with the size from KVM_GET_VCPU_MMAP_SIZE. The VMM calls KVM_RUN in a loop and inspects exit_reason when it returns.

scenes.caption: Only exits KVM cannot handle in-kernel, like I/O and MMIO, return to userspace.
scenes.narration: Many exits, like EPT faults and CPUID, are handled inside the kernel. Only device emulation, such as port I/O and MMIO, returns to the VMM through KVM_RUN.

elements.text: That split keeps most exits cheap.

takeaway: A VMM is a thin ioctl loop: create VM, give it memory, create vCPUs, and call KVM_RUN until an exit needs device emulation.
